# Pepsi's new retro logo and the evolution of an icon as seen on the American roadside

### Exploring the open-air museum -- America -- that charts Pepsi's design evolution on its 125th anniversary.

[![Image 3: Rolando Pujol's avatar]]

[Rolando Pujol]

Oct 27, 2023

∙ Paid

5

1

1

Share

[![Image 4]]

One of the reasons Coke is “The Real Thing” is that it doesn’t mess with its identity too much. Well, there was that fiasco of New Coke in 1985, but it’s worthy of note that Coke used that imbroglio to double down on its iconography with its Coca-Cola Classic rebrand of the original formula.

Right about now, you might be asking, “Isn’t this post about Pepsi?” It is indeed, but you can’t do a post about Pepsi without tackling its relationship with Coke, and their forever rivalry, once a heated weapon dance at the height of the 1980s Cola Wars.

Pepsi is the perpetual Avis Car Rental of the Cola Wars (We try harder!) and so it often finds itself poking the bear that’s headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia. You know, the Pepsi Challenge. With New Coke in 1985, Pepsi, around then “The Choice of a New Generation,” had Coke on the run for a hot minute. Pepsi had some serious marketing momentum in those years, and that was the era when the Pepsi logo I miss so much was at its zenith.

The official story goes that the logo was rolled out about 1973, according to most accounts, though it is derivative of an earlier one — an intermediary logo — that no longer featured the bottlecap background. (I’ll get into this more below.)

[![Image 5]]

What is often described as the 1973 logo was already appearing in advertising and cartons as early as 1969. This is an excerpt from an ad in the Taylorville Daily Breeze Courier published Dec. 22, 1969. (newspapers.com)

But much to my shock, _**the 1973 logo is actually the 1969 logo!**_ In my research for this post, I discovered that the logo was being used in advertising, but not as the dominant logo, as early as October 1969, four years before it is said to have emerged as the overarching symbol of Pepsi. This really surprised me. It’s almost as if Pepsi was testing out this logo. When you see it, used in a subsidiary fashion, it jumps out at you. You wonder why it’s not front and center because it certainly deserves to be.

1969 was an interesting year, the coda of a decade when corporations were modernizing their identities, reducing them to their essence — clean symbols that would be widely and quickly recognized. The most famous example of this — and undoubtedly the most successful — was Saul Bass’ 1969 redesign of the Bell System logo. Just five years earlier, the company had introduced a simplified Bell, but still, very clearly a Bell, a first step in the dismantling of the fussy 1939 logo.

The 1969 logo reduced the Bell to a sleek, easy-to-grasp symbol, a modernist emblem that needed no explanation and no words. You saw it all by itself, and you grasped what it was. To this day, I am so sad that all the former Bell companies have abandoned the logo, with Verizon maintaining a vestigial use for legal reasons, at this point in phone books nobody uses.

I mention Bass’ logo because the Pepsi Globe logo distilled decades of iconography into a clean sphere, a potent symbol that could stand alone. You could easily lose the word Pepsi and know what the symbol stood for.

[![Image 6]]

The updated 1987 Globe typeface and the new 1991 look. (newspapers.com)

Pepsi updated the logo slightly in 1987, changing the typeface to give it a more futuristic look, and then, in the fall of 1991, the design meddling began when they rolled out a replacement for the simple Pepsi Globe, the word Pepsi separated from the sphere. The Globe and the word PEPSI would be in each other’s orbit, but not together again, for the next 32 years. The design tinkering continued twice a decade or so, and by 2008, Pepsi changed the color scheme to a pale blue, introduced a slender typeface, and put the Pepsi globe on its side, which came to be known as “the smile.”

I frowned.

But Pepsi always knew it had something in that 1970s logo and periodically would revive it on its Pepsi Throwback cans and bottles, seen below on shelves in 2018.

[![Image 7]]

There was excitement and energy around that discarded logo, and when Pepsi recently began to toy with its image again, that 1970s version was clearly a wellspring of inspiration.

And so the recently introduced redesign returns Pepsi to that simple circle, reuniting the word PEPSI with the Globe. There are notable differences, of course, including color and typeface, but it’s clear that we are seeing Pepsi assert its heritage again, finding what’s iconic and enduring about its imagery. I love seeing the word PEPSI back in the white space of the red, white, and blue sphere and using a bold typeface.

So why not just bring back the 1970s logo? I suppose they could have done that, much like Pizza Hut did with the return of its 1974 logo in 2019.

But Pepsi took a “Burger King approach” here, revealing a “retro” logo that is a clear descendant of the beloved 1970s original. This is the kind of Pepsi logo we may have arrived at anyway had the design decisions made between 1991 and 2008 never happened. It’s a fresh take on a classic, forward-looking while respectful of the past.

The smile is now on my face, not on the logo.

[![Image 8]]

The 2023 is crowding out the 2008 version on supermarket shelves. (Rolando Pujol)

The American roadside offers a free museum where you can chart the evolution of the Pepsi symbol, and here are some fine examples you can find from coast to coast.

_**NOTE:**_ This is not meant to be a definitive history of the logo. Rather, it reflects those logos that can be found in the wild. You won’t, for instance, see Brad’s Drink, the first name of this cola, born in New Bern, North Carolina, at Caleb Bradham’s drug store. But it’s a pretty comprehensive look at what’s out there from 1940 to today. (Interesting fact: You can see the earliest iteration of the Pepsi-Cola logo on **[Bradham’s grave]**.)

****

### _**The script wordmark logo**_

## **Pepsi-Cola neon sign, Long Island City**

[![Image 9]]

The iconic Pepsi-Cola sign in Long Island City (Rolando Pujol)

Versions of this logo date back to the late 1890s. The above reflects how the logo looked in 1940.

This massive sign in the Queens neighborhood of Long Island City is a holdover of the now-posh neighborhood’s industrial past. The original version of the sign was installed in 1940 — not 1936, as cited in multiple reports — reflecting the era when the script logo featured a hyphen rather than a dash between the words PEPSI and COLA and an extended fancy flourish on the top of the letter C. An earlier version had the word DRINK in that flourish.

[![Image 10]]

The 1973 logo, a forefather of the 2023 version that was just rolled out. (Rolando Pujol)

Artkraft Strauss reconstructed the sign itself in the 1990s. (A version of the 1970s bottle had replaced an earlier one.) Pepsi’s plant closed here in 2003, but the sign would find a new home at Gantry Plaza State Park nearby.

[![Image 11]]

I took this shot of the sign from Manhattan back in 2008. 

It was designated a New York City landmark in 2016. **[See the designation report]**, as well as a photo of the sign from 1988, when it still stood atop the Pepsi factory. Interestingly, Pepsi still maintains the sign.**[[MAP]]**

## **Pepsi-Cola sign, the Bronx**

Interestingly, a longtime Pepsi bottling plant in the Bronx earlier this year installed a few signs, including one apparently lit with neon (!!!!), with what is a modified version of the cursive logo. The first indication I’ve seen of this simplified logo in newspaper archives is not 1940, as many logo sites report, but 1951, embedded in the Pepsi bottlecap logo. The equal sign was replaced with a hyphen, and some of the fanciful type flourishes were curtailed. It’s a good deal cleaner and crisper.

It was a wonderful surprise to see this logo on the Bronx facility, as this bottling plant has never had a Pepsi logo to my memory.[]**[[MAP]]**

[![Image 12]]

If I didn’t know better, I’d say these signs in the Bronx had been there for decades. Instead, they were just installed this year. (Rolando Pujol)

[![Image 13]]

## **Pepsi-Cola sign, Hyattsville, Maryland**

A cousin of this sign can be found at the Pepsi Bottling Group building in Hyattsville, Maryland. I’ve stopped at various times of day to capture it. **[[MAP]]**

Under this name, it was only served within his pharmacy; a logo was not drafted for it until the name was changed and the syrup began being distributed in 1898. * '''NOTE:''' The ornamented logo widely claimed as the beverage's first logo was never used in any capacity by Caleb Bradham or his company. It originates from the cover of '''', a 1976 Pepsi collectors' guide. An edited version of the cover with the subtitle of the book airbrushed out was once touted online as a legitimate advertisement, but has since been debunked. The typeface used, Filmotype Quentin, was not designed until the late 1950s. ==Pepsi-Cola / Pepsi== =1898–1903= [[File:Pepsi 1898.svg|center|300px]] On August 28, 1898, Brad's Drink began being marketed as '''Pepsi-Cola,''' due to its original selling point of "curing" dyspepsia, the medical term for indigestion.https://www.foodandwine.com/origin-of-the-name-pepsi-8407398 =1903–1904= [[File:Pepsi 1903.svg|center|300px]] =1904–1905= [[File:Pepsi 1904.svg|center|300px]] =1905–1906= [[File:Pepsi 1905.svg|center|250px]] Though a trademark for this design was filed in 1905, no contemporary sources for this logo other than said filing are known to survive today; however, it appears regularly on nostalgia merchandise. =1906–1934= [[File:Pepsi - 1906.svg|center|300px]] ==1915–1916== [[File:Pepsi-Cola - 1915.png|center|350px]] Beginning in 1915, a rough sans-serif wordmark (similar to Berthold Block) would be consistently used in advertising. ==1916–1920== [[File:Pepsi-Cola - 1916.png|center|350px]] ==1920–1922== [[File:Pepsi - 1920.png|center|350px]] {{SVG needed}} Informal "fat face" renderings of the Pepsi-Cola name with elongated initials were used on signage and advertising for a brief period in the early 1920s, but never appeared on the product itself. =1934–1951= [[File:Pepsi 1934.svg|center|300px]] =1951–1962, 1962–1971 (bottles only), 2008–2009, 2014-present= [[File:Pepsi - 1951.svg|center|300px]] In August 1951, Pepsi-Cola introduced the first major change to its script in 45 years. Use of the plain script logo in most advertising was halted in 1962, save for the reverse side of Pepsi bottles, until 1971. In 2008, the launch of [[Pepsi Throwback]] saw this logo make a brief return until it was replaced with a modified version of the 1971 logo a year later. In 2014, it was reintroduced for the now renamed [[Pepsi-Cola Made with Real Sugar]] and has been used for that ever since; it's also seen on the back of all cans and bottles of the mainline Pepsi brand since then for trademark upkeep purposes. ==1951–1962, 1962–1969 (cartons only), 2004== [[File:1950-Pepsi-Logo.svg|center|200px]] This logo, sometimes viewed as an alternate, was launched alongside the cap-less script logo and actually used at about the same frequency. Most notable about this logo is that it was the first Pepsi used that carried the swirled "Globe" motif, which has been a part of the drink's design language ever since. The bottle cap variation continued to be used on the ends of 6-pack cartons until 1969's total packaging redesign. It was brought back in 2004 for [[Pepsi Holiday Spice]]. =1962–1970= ==1962–1965== Pepsi - 1962 (cap).svg| Pepsi - 1962c.svg| This updated bottle cap logo featuring a modern sans-serif typeface was introduced in 1962. The version with the shortened "Pepsi" name would be introduced in December 1962, to first be used on the company's ''Crown Line'' vending machines. ==1965-1970== Pepsi - 1965.svg| Pepsi-Cola - 1962.svg| {{Card|designer=Jerome Gould of
[[Gould & Associates]]|type=Custom|date=September 1965}} In 1965, a simplified version was phased in omitting the crown design in favor of the swirls alone. It was during this period that the Pepsi name began to outpace "Pepsi-Cola" in advertising. =1969–1991, 2009–2014, 2019= ==1969–1987== {{Bg|[[File:Pepsi - 1969.svg|center|250px]]}} {{Card|designer=Jerome Gould of
[[Gould & Associates]]|type=Custom|date=October 1969}} A modernized logo was introduced on redesigned cartons and 32-oz bottle labels in late 1969. Bottles still used a combination of the 1962-1971 serif "Pepsi" wordmark and the 1951 script logo during this period. ==1970–1987, 1981–1991 (China), 2009–2014, 2019== [[File:Pepsi - 1973.svg|center|300px]] {{Card|designer=Frank B. Rupp|type=Custom|date=October 1970}} In late 1970, this logo fully replaced the 1951 script logo and the 1962 serif logo on bottles in a massive redesign campaign that swept all aspects of the brand. A recreation of this logo was used by [[Pepsi Throwback]] from 2009 until its renaming in 2014. It was also used for a short time in 2019 for the Joy of Pepsi promotion. ==1987–1991== [[File:Pepsi Logo 1980s.svg|center|300px]] {{Card|type=Handel Gothic (modified)|date=January 1, 1987}} Following the well-received redesign of [[Diet Pepsi]] in 1986, the 15-year incumbent logo was modernized to match. The previously "grotesk" type style was changed to a geometric sans serif. A registered trademark symbol was generally nested under the bowl of the second "P". Cans produced in January 1987 commemorating the Rutan Voyager's non-stop worldwide flight the month prior were among the earliest known to carry this logo. =1991–1997, 1991–1996 (international), 1991–1998 (China)= [[File:Pepsi logo 1991.svg|center|300px]] {{Card|designer=[[Peterson & Blyth Associates]]|date=September 22, 1991|type=Handel Gothic (modified)}} In September 1991, a radically altered new logo was introduced, keeping the modern type style and swirls but changing their relationship to each other. This marks the first time that the "Pepsi" text was used apart from between the swirls. The white line between the red and blue swirls was also thinned to be more graphic, a move made by [[Diet Pepsi#1985-1991|Diet Pepsi six years prior]]. The italicized text and rectangular shape suggests excitement. * =1996–1998 (international)= [[File:Pepsi 1996.svg|center|300px]] {{Card|designer=[[Landor Associates]]|type=Handel Gothic|date=April 1996}} In April 1996, Pepsi launched ''Project Blue'' in some international markets outside the United States. The launch included extravagant publicity stunts, such as a Concorde airplane owned by [[Air France]] painted in blue colors as well as a banner on the Mir space station. * =1997–2003, 1998–2003 (international)= [[File:Pepsi (1998).svg|center|300px]] {{Card|designer=Unknown|type=Handel Gothic (modified)|date=December 1997}} A new logo similar to that of ''Project Blue'' was introduced in the U.S. in December 1997, a year before Pepsi's centennial year began. It was at this point that the logo began to be referred to as the Pepsi Globe. From May to September 2018, this logo was temporarily brought back alongside the 1991 and 1971 logos (and used on 355ml cans everywhere as well as 591ml bottles in the US only) for Pepsi's music generations campaign. It remained on the ''Pepsi Max Big One'' ride at [[Pleasure Beach Resort]] until 2012. * =2003–2008, 2003–2014 (international)= ==2003–2006, 2003–2014 (international), 2004–2008 (Georgia)== [[File:Pepsi 2003.svg|center|250px]] * {{Card|designer=[[Landor Associates]]|date=February 4, 2003|font=Serpentine (modified)}} On February 4, 2003, a new logo was launched with a more modern, block letter type style and the Pepsi ball rendered three-dimensionally. It didn't last long until it was modified once again, three years after its launch. After the 2008 logo was unveiled, [[Pepsi Zero Sugar|Diet Pepsi Max]] continued to use this logo until its name change to Pepsi Max in North America in 2009. [[Pepsi Wild Cherry]] used this logo until March 2010, and [[Pepsi One]] was the last variant to continue using this logo; it switched to the 2008 logo around late 2012. Many countries outside the US still used this logo through 2010. Mainland China still used this logo until 2014. ==2006–2008, 2006–2010 (international)== [[File:Pepsi (2006) stacked.svg|center|230px]] {{Card|date=June 2, 2006|font=Serpentine}} On June 2, 2006, Pepsi slightly modified the 2003 logo by moving the text below the globe. # The Pepsi Logo History, Colors, Font, And Meaning

![Image 3]

[Bogdan Sandu]Designer & Founder

 19 December 2025 

 11 min read 

![Image 4: The Pepsi Logo History, Colors, Font, And Meaning]

The Pepsi logo stands as one of the most recognizable brand symbols in the beverage industry. This circular emblem, known as the Pepsi Globe, has gone through numerous transformations since the company’s founding in 1893.

PepsiCo currently uses a modernized version introduced in 2023. The design features the iconic red, white, and blue color scheme that has defined the brand for decades.

What makes this [logo] particularly interesting is its ability to stay relevant while maintaining core visual elements. The brand has cycled through approximately 12 major logo iterations. Each redesign reflected changing design trends and marketing strategies of its era.

## What Is the Pepsi Logo?

![Image 5]

The Pepsi logo is a circular emblem featuring a red, white, and blue globe divided by a wavy white band. Introduced in its current form in 2023, this combination mark was redesigned by PepsiCo’s in-house team. The symbol represents energy, youthfulness, and American heritage.

### Design Specifications

* **Design Type:** Combination mark (symbol plus wordmark)
* **Primary Elements:** Circular globe icon with tricolor scheme, custom wordmark
* **Official Introduction Date:** March 2023 (current version)
* **Designer/Agency:** PepsiCo in-house design team
* **Trademark Status:** Registered trademark of PepsiCo, Inc.
* **Color Palette:** Electric Blue (#005EEF), Pepsi Red (#EB0029), White (#FFFFFF), Black (#000000)
* **Usage Context:** Product packaging, digital platforms, advertising, merchandise, retail displays, corporate communications

## How Has the Pepsi Logo Evolved Over Time?

![Image 6]

The Pepsi logo has undergone 12 major redesigns since 1898. Early versions featured ornate Victorian lettering.

The 1940s introduced the bottle cap design. The 1970s brought minimalist approaches.

The 2008 redesign sparked controversy with its tilted globe. The 2023 update returned to bolder, more confident styling.

### Original Pepsi-Cola Logo (1898-1905)

* **Years Active:** 1898-1905
* **Design Description:** Red script lettering spelling “Pepsi-Cola” in an elaborate Victorian style
* **Color Scheme:** Red on white background
* **Designer:** Caleb Bradham (founder)
* **Context:** Created when the drink was renamed from “Brad’s Drink” to Pepsi-Cola
* **Key Changes from Previous:** First official logo design
* **Cultural Significance:** Established the brand’s initial visual identity during the patent medicine era

### Refined Script Logo (1905-1940)

* **Years Active:** 1905-1940
* **Design Description:** More elaborate red [script font] with swirling flourishes
* **Color Scheme:** Deep red lettering
* **Designer:** Unknown
* **Context:** Reflected the ornamental design trends of the early 20th century
* **Key Changes from Previous:** Added decorative elements and refined letterforms
* **Cultural Significance:** Positioned Pepsi as a premium soda fountain drink

### Bottle Cap Era Logo (1940-1950)

* **Years Active:** 1940-1950
* **Design Description:** First appearance of the red, white, and blue color scheme in a bottle cap format
* **Color Scheme:** Red, white, and blue
* **Designer:** Unknown
* **Context:** Introduced during World War II to express patriotic sentiment
* **Key Changes from Previous:** Added blue color, created circular bottle cap shape
* **Cultural Significance:** Aligned the brand with American patriotism during wartime

### Streamlined Globe Logo (1950-1962)

* **Years Active:** 1950-1962
* **Design Description:** Refined bottle cap design with cleaner lines and “Pepsi-Cola” script
* **Color Scheme:** Red, white, blue
* **Designer:** Unknown
* **Context:** Post-war optimism and mid-century modern design influence
* **Key Changes from Previous:** Simplified forms, more readable typography
* **Cultural Significance:** Reflected America’s post-war prosperity and confidence

### Pepsi Generation Logo (1962-1973)

![Image 7]

* **Years Active:** 1962-1973
* **Design Description:** Simplified globe with “Pepsi” in a [sans-serif font], dropping “Cola” from the name
* **Color Scheme:** Red, white, blue
* **Designer:** Unknown
* **Context:** Launched alongside the “Pepsi Generation” marketing campaign targeting youth
* **Key Changes from Previous:** Dropped “Cola” from the logo, modernized typography
* **Cultural Significance:** Marked Pepsi’s shift toward youth culture marketing

### Globe Refinement Logo (1973-1991)

* **Years Active:** 1973-1991
* **Design Description:** Boxed globe design with uppercase “PEPSI” lettering
* **Color Scheme:** Red, white, blue with bolder tones
* **Designer:** Landor Associates
* **Context:** Corporate identity standardization era
* **Key Changes from Previous:** Introduced rectangular framing, uppercase letters
* **Cultural Significance:** Represented corporate professionalism and brand consistency

### Circular Globe Logo (1991-1998)

* **Years Active:** 1991-1998
* **Design Description:** Three-dimensional globe effect with italicized “PEPSI” wordmark
* **Color Scheme:** Red, white, blue with dimensional shading
* **Designer:** Landor Associates
* **Context:** Digital age influence, 3D graphics becoming popular
* **Key Changes from Previous:** Added depth and dimension, italicized text
* **Cultural Significance:** Reflected the emerging digital aesthetic of the 1990s

### Millennium Globe Logo (1998-2008)

* **Years Active:** 1998-2008
* **Design Description:** Glossy 3D globe with lowercase “pepsi” in a rounded font
* **Color Scheme:** Brighter red, white, blue with [gradient] effects
* **Designer:** Unknown

# History of the Pepsi Logo

* * *

Posted on September 23rd 2018

![Image 1: The History of the Pepsi Logo]

Pepsi is one of the most globally recognized logos in the world. Its rich history spans over a century and its current form is the culmination of many changes - a constant exercise in progressive minimalism as the company strives to keep its image relevant for every generation.

![Image 2]
Probably the most surprising aspect of Pepsi’s brand is that it wasn’t always called Pepsi. In 1893, a pharmacist named Caleb Bradham created a beverage made of sugar, water, caramel, lemon oil, nutmeg, and other natural additives. He sold it at his pharmacy in New Bern, North Carolina under the name “Brad’s Drink” which enjoyed instant local success.

## Pepsi Cola is Born

![Image 3]
On August 28, 1898, Bradham renamed his drink “Pepsi-Cola”. He peddled his drink as more than mere refreshment, but a healthy beverage, aiding in digestion and boosting energy levels. He also knew he needed a new name to achieve mainstream success. By this time, Coca Cola had already become an overnight sensation, so it’s not surprising that he wanted to go in a very similar direction.

## 1905 Rebrand

![Image 4]
In 1905 the brand would undergo its first revision, clearly an attempt to make the logo more legible and smooth. The use of a bolder script font and elimination of ornamental decorations ensured a much stronger brand presence.

## 1906 Rebrand

![Image 5]
The script font is modified and made bolder for more simplicity. At this time the company touted the slogan, “The Original Pure Food Drink.”, which is why the word “Drink” was also incorporated into the wordmark. This particular version would prove to endure longer than any of its predecessors, remaining unmodified for almost four decades.

## 1940 Rebrand

![Image 6]
It is now 1940 and Pepsi Cola has grown into an international brand. During an era where the concept of global marketing and branding is becoming more commonplace, the creative team is ready for another logo revision. The font still uses serifs but they are minimized, along with any decorative flair that may have survived from earlier iterations.

## 1950 Rebrand

![Image 7]
In the wake of World War 2, patriotic feelings in the United States are at an all-time high. With the addition of blue, a patriotic color palette is attained, along with an iconic bottle camp which would endure for 12 years.

## 1962 Rebrand

![Image 8]
The logo was updated to read simply “PEPSI” in a bold, sans serif font, this time superimposed on the classic bottle cap but from a straight perspective, making the logo more symmetrical and iconic. It’s also around this time that “Pepsi Generation” as a concept is pushed via radio spots and song writing contests.

## 1973 Rebrand

![Image 9]
The success of the previous logo has now been distilled to a bare minimum. The same font is used but the classic bottle cap has been hyper minimalized within this famous boxed-in version of the company’s brand. This is also the first time a third color is added, with sky blue becoming a staple of the logo and marketing materials.

## 1987 Rebrand

![Image 10]
While the visual layout from 1973 is preserved, this is the first time Pepsi uses an unconventional and modern custom typeface that will help the company’s image as innovative and future-minded.

## 1991 Rebrand

![Image 11]
Pepsi is thinking outside the box, liberating both its wordmark and bottlecap icon from the previous layout and letting them exist in their own spaces. The custom font has also been tweaked with a 12 degree italic slant, another visual indication of the company’s forward thinking and vision.

## 1998 Rebrand

![Image 12]
Striving towards more boldness and simplicity, Pepsi eliminates the red box completely so the wordmark and icon stand out more. The move towards a blue as the dominant color also helps distinguish the brand from other competitors.

## 2003 Rebrand

![Image 13]
The turn of the millennium has come and gone and the Pepsi logo has been updated with pseudo-serifs reminiscent of its 1940 rebrand, along with some subtle 3D shading.

## 2006 Rebrand

![Image 14]
The wordmark is moved below the circle and the colors are swapped while the icon itself is given further 3D treatment in the form of ice and condensation, a visual hint of how refreshing the beverage can be.

## 2008 Rebrand

![Image 15]
In probably the boldest departure of previous styles, Pepsi unleashes a lower case wordmark in a thin, sans serif font and distorts the cap icon by stretching it over a sphere - a nod to the company’s reach as an global purveyor of commerce and culture.

## 2014 - Present

![Image 16]
In 2014, even more simplicity is achieved as designers opt to remove the blue line around the circle, allowing it to carve its white center from the surrounding negative space.

## Conclusion

It’s pretty amazing how far the branding has come over the last century, having seen the logo change colors and fonts. It’s pretty clear that Pepsi has never been afraid to reinvent itself over and over again, while still remaining a global brand.

## How did it all start for Pepsi?

![Image 13: Cola Company]

Before knowing the Pepsi logo history, let us first find out how the business started. A North Carolina pharmacist, **Caleb D. Bradham** had invented the original Pepsi Cola formula in 1893.

Bradman had installed a soda fountain inside his pharmacy. He served drinks made of the formula to the customers and named his popular drink as **“Brad’s Drink.’’** It was a mix of water, sugar, lemon oil, caramel, nutmeg, kola nuts, and other additives.

With the popularity of the drink increasing, Brad now wanted to have a catchy name for it. So, he eventually named it Pepsi-Cola. He trademarked the title by the summer of 1903. Soon, the soda syrup was all over North California in pharmacies and other stores. The brand proliferated, and by 1910, it had franchises in 24 states.

Today, Pepsi Cola is one of the most famous beverage brands known for its chilling taste worldwide. Its logo has contributed a lot to the success of the company.

Pepsi logo is one of the most recognized logos across the globe. However, it is not appropriate to say that the logo became popular or recognizable due to the beverage’s popularity. The [**packaging design**] of Pepsi has contributed in a big way to the success of the brand.

## How The Pepsi Logo Got Evolved Over the Decades?

### 1893–1898 – The Blue And Bold Font Logo

The first logo of the company was a blue wordmark that read ‘’Brad’s Drink’’. And the wordmark appeared against a white background. The company used a bold font that had some ornamentation to it. This ornate characteristic continued to be part of the Pepsi Logo for many years to come.

![Image 17: Brads-Drink]

### 1898 – Use Of Swirly Script In The Logo

### 1898–1905

On August 28, 1898, the company decided to change its name to Pepsi-Cola from the original Brad’s Drink. Therefore, the Pepsi logo was also radically changed to a swirl symbol.

[![Image 19: Logo Design]]

![Image 21: Pepsi-Cola-Logo]

### 1905–1906

By 1905 the logo started looking similar to its rival Coca-Cola logo. The swirls became bold and thick.

![Image 23: Pepsi-Cola-Logo-1905-1906]

### 1906–1940

In 1906, the Pepsi logo underwent another change in design when the logo incorporated lots of text. The typography of the old Pepsi logo, however, was more or less the same. The logo attained a spherical shape for the first time, which became a significant success.

![Image 25: Pepsi-Cola-Drink]

Also, the spherical shape continues to be part of the design till today. One of the reasons for the spherical shape of the Pepsi logo design was that the company wanted to accommodate the slogan **“The Original Pure Food Drink’’** in the design. The swirl design was unchanged except that the lines became even thicker.

### The 1940s

In the 1940s, Pepsi went back to a rectangular shape for the logo. The letters Pepsi Cola were in a rectangular box that had an entirely white background. The letters were in the red.

So, the contrast of white and red gave the logo its distinctness. But another reason for the vintage Pepsi logo having red and white Pepsi colors was to show support to America’s efforts in World War II. It was because of this support that the logo dropped its curlicues to some extent.

![Image 27: Pepsi Cola logo]

The Pepsi Cola logo got a refined look when the swirled smoothened. By 1943, Pepsi designed its logo in the shape of a bottle cap. The slogan **“Bigger Drink, Better Taste”** was on the cap.

The new logo had clean letters with no elements of edges at the letters. This Pepsi redesign continued with the company for more than 20 years.

### The 1950s – The Bottle Cap Design

In 1950, the company launched a new bottle cap logo. The logo had blue color for the first time. So, a combination of red, blue, and white in the Pepsi logo evoked patriotic feelings following World War II.

![Image 29: Bottle Cap Design]

During the 1950s, Pepsi marketed itself as a brand with better value. Its tagline was “More bounce to the ounce,’’ That was about promising more soda per bottle than the rival Coca-Cola.

### The 1960s – Cola Removed From The Logo

At the beginning of the 1960s, Pepsi made a significant change in its logo. It was the time when the company got rid of the Cola word from the Pepsi-Cola sign. Pepsi borrowed the word Cola from Coca-Cola, which was the leading competitor.
